first_draft.title: Pip and the Falling Stars
first_draft.text:
Pip was a penguin who lived on a bright blue shore. Pip had never seen snow.

One morning, the sky turned soft and gray. Pip looked up. Something white was drifting down. Flick. Flake. Flick.

"What is that?" squawked Pip. "Is the sky crumbling?"

Pip's friend Olu, a wise old seal with a whiskery grin, laughed a deep, rumbly laugh. "That's snow, little one. It falls from the clouds, soft as feathers."

Pip flapped her flippers. "Can I catch some?"

"You can try," said Olu.

Pip waddled up the hill. Waddle, waddle, slide. Waddle, waddle, slide. Her belly went bump on the cold white ground.

She opened her beak wide. Flick! A flake landed on her tongue. Then it was gone. It tasted like nothing at all.

"Oops," said Pip. "It melted before I could hold it."

She tried again. She held out one flipper, very still. Flick. A flake landed on the tip of it. Pip stared. Her flipper was cold and tingly. She looked at the flake, and it did not melt right away. It sat there, a tiny star with six points.

"Olu! Come look! It has corners!"

Olu slid up beside her, slow and careful. He leaned close. "Six little points," he whispered. "Every flake is different."

Pip gasped. She turned to the next flake, and the next. Flick. Flick. Each one had its own shape. Some looked like feathers. Some looked like tiny snowy trees.

"Snow is so busy," said Pip. "But it is so quiet, too."

Then the flakes began to pile up. The hill grew soft and round. Pip sank in up to her knees. Crunch. Squeak. Crunch.

"Let's make something!" said Olu.

They packed the snow into a big round ball. It was lumpy and wobbly. Pip pressed two pebbles in for eyes. Olu gave it a crooked stick for a nose.

"Hello, Snowy Pip," said Pip, and she giggled so hard she hiccupped. Hic! Her hiccup echoed across the hill.

The sky grew dim and blue. The snow kept falling, soft and slow. Flick. Flake. Flick.

Pip yawned a long, wide yawn. Her flippers felt heavy and warm.

"Time to go home, little one," said Olu.

Pip waddled down the hill, one slow step at a time. Behind her, the snow settled over the footprints, as gentle as a blanket.

She tucked her beak under her wing. The snow kept falling. Flick. Flake. Hush.

Good night, Pip. Good night, snow.

Behind her, the snow settled over the footprints, as gentle as a blanket.

She tucked her beak under her wing. The snow kept falling. Flick. Flake. Hush.

Good night, Pip. Good night, snow.

first_draft.title: Noor and Wenceslas and the Wobbly Fort
first_draft.text:
On a rainy Saturday, Noor and her twin brother, Wenceslas, dragged every blanket in the house into the living room. The sofa cushions thumped onto the rug. The curtains swished like tired ghosts. Noor had a plan, and every good plan needed a secret code. She tapped on the arm of the armchair: three quick taps, a pause, then two slow ones. "That means FORT," she whispered. "Only twins know it."

Wenceslas tapped back, grinning so wide his freckles squished together. Then his nose wiggled. His eyes squeezed shut. "Ah... ah... KER-CHOOOO!"

The blanket roof sighed, wobbled, and slid sideways, flopping onto Noor's head like a wet pancake.

"Wenceslas!" she squeaked from under the wool.

"Sorry," he said. "The dust tickles."

They tried again. They pulled two dining chairs together and draped the biggest blanket over the top. It sagged in the middle like a tired camel. Wenceslas poked it. Boing. It sagged even lower.

"We need a pole," Noor said, tapping her chin. "Something tall and strong to hold the roof up."

Wenceslas looked around. He found the mop. Noor shook her head. He found the umbrella stand. Noor shook her head again. Then he found the broom, and Noor's eyes lit up.

"The broom!" they said together, then giggled, because they always said things together.

They rested the broom across the chair backs, like the pole of a tent. The blanket rose up, proud and tall. But the corners kept flapping free, like pirate flags in a breeze.

"Hold on," said Noor. "We need heavy things to keep the corners down."

She fetched the atlas, the dictionary and Grandma's cookbook. The cookbook landed with a sound like a sleeping hippo. Thump. Thump. Thump. Each corner stayed put.

Wenceslas took a deep breath, and his nose twitched. Everyone waited. "Ah... ah..." He pinched his nose hard. "...ahh... no. Not this time!" The roof trembled, then stood firm as a castle wall.

Noor pulled the torch from the drawer. She switched off the big light. Click. A warm yellow circle danced across the blanket walls. Their shadow hands became rabbits, then a dragon with a wobbly tail.

"Crawl in," she whispered. "Code's FORT."

Inside, everything was soft and hushed. The blankets glowed red and gold. Wenceslas whispered, "Is this our castle?"

"It's our castle," said Noor. "And it's a secret."

Mum's head popped through the gap. "Is that a castle or a laundry explosion?" she asked, smiling. She held two mugs of warm milk. "The roof looks very strong," she said. She set the mugs on the rug, kissed the tops of their heads, and tiptoed away.

The milk was warm and sweet. They sipped and giggled until their giggles turned into yawns.

"Do you think the fort will still be here tomorrow?" Wenceslas asked.

Noor snuggled deeper into her sleeping bag. "Forts don't go anywhere. They wait for us."

The torch clicked off. The room went soft and dark. Outside, rain tapped gently on the window. Noor's eyes grew heavy. Wenceslas breathed slow and quiet, in and out, in and out.

"Night, fort," whispered Noor.

"Shh," breathed Wenceslas. "Ah... ah..." He pressed his nose into his pillow. "...ahh... no sneeze."

The blanket roof did not move at all.

request: A robot vacuum cleaner who is scared of the family cat

first_draft.title: Thaddeus and the Very Brave Crumb Hunt
first_draft.text:
Thaddeus was a robot vacuum with round blue eyes, a whirring belly, and a very loud case of the jitters. Every morning he rolled out of his charging dock in the hallway, went bump, bonk, whirrr across the rugs, and every morning he saw the cat.

The cat was named Nubbin. She was a fat, fluffy, marmalade-colored cat with a tail shaped like a curly question mark. She sat on the windowsill in a warm patch of sunshine, and when Thaddeus came near, she opened one golden eye and said, "Mrrrp?"

"EEEK!" squeaked Thaddeus. He spun in a circle so fast that he bumped into the umbrella stand. Clonk. Clatter. Boing.

Ulla came running down the hall in her socks, which never matched. She was seven, and she had a gap in her front teeth. "Thaddeus, you have to finish the living room," she said. "Mum says the crumbs are having a party."

"I cannot," whispered Thaddeus. "Nubbin might pounce. She has claws. Twenty of them, and they are probably very sharp."

Ulla giggled. "Nubbin's claws are only for scratching the sofa. She's far too lazy to pounce on anything except a sunbeam."

So Thaddeus tried. First he rolled in backwards, very slowly, beeping a tiny song. Nubbin yawned, stretched, and Thaddeus shrieked, "EEEK!" and reversed into the bookcase. Next he wore a tea towel as a cape and tiptoed in, pretending to be a mysterious shadow. Nubbin sneezed. Thaddeus fell over with a clunk and lay upside down, his wheels spinning in the air. "Bloop," he sighed. "Nobody is scared of a shadow with a cape."

Then Ulla rolled a ball of pink yarn across the floor. It bounced, wobbled, and rolled under the sofa, right next to the spot where Nubbin liked to sleep. Nubbin's whiskers twitched. She stood up, looked at the yarn, and then looked at Thaddeus. Thaddeus switched on his fan to clean the crumbs, and the whirr went WHRRRRRR. Nubbin leapt straight behind the curtain and trembled.

Thaddeus stopped. "Ulla," he said slowly, "I think she is scared of me."

"Of course she is," said Ulla. "You're loud and you go bonk into things."

Thaddeus thought about this. He switched off his fan. He rolled forward, one tiny wheel at a time. "Hello, Nubbin," he whispered. "I am a vacuum, not a monster. I only eat crumbs. Crumbs taste terrible, I think."

first_draft.title: Jonah and the Owl Who Forgot to Hoot
first_draft.text:
Jonah sat on the bottom stair and listened to his house. Upstairs, a brand-new crib went creak. In the kitchen, the kettle went whooo. Soon there would be a baby sister, with tiny socks and a tiny crying sound and so much new.

"Will there be time for me?" Jonah asked. His voice came out small, like a mouse in a sock.

Mom sat down beside him. Her cardigan smelled of toast and lavender. "That's a big question. Let's think about it together."

Jonah thought hard, with his tongue poking out the side of his mouth. "Maybe I could help. I could carry the wipes. I could hold the tiny socks."

"That would be a great help," said Mom. "But big brothers are allowed to need help too."

That week, Jonah tried very hard. He carried wipes up the stairs one at a time. Thump, thump, thump, went the wipes. He sorted socks by color: red, blue, and one lonely yellow. He made a wobbly tower of diapers, and it fell down with a plop, plop, plop, and he laughed until he hiccupped.

Then one evening, the baby began to cry. Dad was running a bath with a splish-splash-splosh. Mom was rocking the baby with a shh, shh, shh. Jonah stood in the hall with a sock in each hand. Nobody looked up.

His chin wobbled. He wanted to shout, "Me! Me! Me!" But a shout might wake the baby. So he sat on the top step and hugged his knees.

Soon Dad's socks came padding along the hall. Dad sat down next to him, dripping a little. "Hello, Captain Jonah. Did you know your mom and I have a list?"

"A list?"

"A list of things only Jonah can do." Dad counted on his fingers. "Only you can tell the silliest knock-knock jokes. Only you can make Mom snort her cocoa. Only you know exactly where the flashlight lives."

Jonah sniffed. "What about bedtime?"

"Bedtime is yours," said Dad. "Every night, you pick a book. After the baby's asleep, it's your story. Nobody else gets to read it."

Jonah's chin stopped wobbling. He picked the book about the owl who forgot how to hoot. That night, he sat close to Mom on the rug. He read in his best owl voice. Hoo-hoo, said Jonah. Hoo-hoo, said Mom, and then they both laughed in whispers.

From the crib came a little gurgle. Jonah peeked over the edge. His baby sister had one fist by her ear and a sleepy frown on her face.

"Night, Sorrel," Jonah whispered. "I'll read you the owl story tomorrow."

Mom kissed the top of his head. "You know what, Jonah? Love isn't like milk in a jug. It doesn't run out when you pour some for somebody new."

The kettle went quiet. The crib stopped creaking. The bath drain gave one last gurgle and then hushed. The hall light made a soft yellow stripe on the floor.

Jonah pulled his blanket up to his chin. His eyes felt heavy, like warm pillows. Somewhere, a tiny sister breathed in and out, in and out.

Goodnight, Jonah. Goodnight, Sorrel. Goodnight, house.

first_draft.title: Ramona, Basil and the Confetti Cannons
first_draft.text:
The sea lay as flat as a pancake the morning two pirate ships sailed into Coconut Bay, and neither captain was in a friendly mood.

On the left sailed the Salty Biscuit, captained by Ramona Stroud, who wore a red bandana and spoke in a voice like a foghorn. On the right sailed the Brine Gull, captained by Basil Thorne, who wore three hats at once and was very proud of his moustache.

"That treasure map is mine!" bellowed Ramona. "You swiped it from my sea chest!"

"Swiped?" spluttered Basil, waving a crinkled scrap of parchment. "I found it floating in a bottle, fair and square!"

Gulls wheeled overhead. On the Salty Biscuit, a parrot squawked, "Shiver my timbers! Shiver my timbers!"

"Man the cannons!" roared Ramona.

"Man the cannons!" roared Basil, not to be outdone.

Two cannons went off with a tremendous BOOM. But out burst no cannonballs, only a fountain of rainbow confetti. It drifted down over both decks like a sparkly snowfall and settled on Basil's hats until he looked like a birthday cake.

Ramona's crew giggled. Basil's crew giggled louder. Even the parrot joined in with a hiccup.

"Cheating!" cried Basil, flicking streamers from his moustache. "Swords, then! Let the duel decide!"

Wooden practice swords clacked and clattered. Basil lunged, tripped over a coil of rope, and sat down with a squishy plop in a barrel of soap bubbles. Ramona slipped on the bubbles, and both captains tumbled across the deck, laughing so hard they could barely breathe.

That was when a small brown crab came scuttling along the planks, with the treasure map clutched in one claw.

"Oi! Give that back!" shouted both captains at once.

The crab only snapped its claws and scuttled down the gangplank onto the sand. Captain Ramona and Captain Basil raced after it, hopping over shells and splashing through the shallows, while their crews cheered from the rails.

At the foot of a palm tree, the crab dropped the parchment and vanished into a rock pool.

Ramona picked it up. The map was torn clean down the middle. Basil pulled a ragged half from inside his waistcoat. "Well, blow me down," whispered Ramona.

The two halves fitted together like puzzle pieces. A golden X shone right beneath the palm tree.

"We've been squabbling over half a map," said Basil, and his moustache drooped.

"Then let's share the other half," said Ramona, and she offered him her hand.

They dug with two spades, one from each ship. Sand flew, crabs scuttled, and a few minutes later, clunk! Their spades struck a wooden chest. Inside lay sacks of gold coins, and a hundred chocolate ones wrapped in shiny foil.

"Fifty each," said Ramona, counting carefully. "And the chocolate goes to whoever can sing the loudest shanty."

Both crews sang so badly that the gulls flew away, and the parrot ended up in a sulk.

As the sun sank behind the palm trees, the two ships rocked gently side by side at anchor. Lanterns glowed like tiny moons.

Ramona yawned, and Basil yawned back, and the parrot tucked its head beneath one wing.

Hush now. The waves are soft, the confetti is sleepy, and the sea is rocking everyone to rest.

Goodnight, sailors. Goodnight, sea.

final.title: Ramona, Basil and the Confetti Cannons
final.text:
The sea lay as flat as a pancake the morning two pirate ships sailed into Coconut Bay, and neither captain was in a friendly mood.

On the left sailed the Salty Biscuit, captained by Ramona Stroud, who wore a red bandana and spoke in a voice like a foghorn. On the right sailed the Brine Gull, captained by Basil Thorne, who wore three hats at once and was very proud of his moustache.

"That treasure map is mine!" bellowed Ramona. "You swiped it from my sea chest!"

"Swiped?" spluttered Basil, waving a crinkled scrap of parchment. "I found it floating in a bottle, fair and square!"

Gulls wheeled overhead. On the Salty Biscuit, a parrot squawked, "Shiver my timbers! Shiver my timbers!"

"Man the cannons!" roared Ramona.

"Man the cannons!" roared Basil, not to be outdone.

Two cannons went off with a tremendous BOOM. But out burst no cannonballs, only a fountain of rainbow confetti. It drifted down over both decks like a sparkly snowfall and settled on Basil's hats until he looked like a birthday cake.

Ramona's crew giggled. Basil's crew giggled louder. Even the parrot joined in with a hiccup.

"Cheating!" cried Basil, flicking streamers from his moustache. "Swords, then! Let the duel decide!"

Wooden practice swords clacked and clattered. Basil lunged, tripped over a coil of rope, and sat down with a squishy plop in a barrel of soap bubbles. Ramona slipped on the bubbles, and both captains tumbled across the deck, laughing so hard they could barely breathe.

That was when a small brown crab came scuttling along the planks. It snatched the parchment from Basil's hand and tore it clean down the middle. Then it scurried off with one half clutched in its claw, while Basil stood there holding the other.

"Oi! Give that back!" shouted both captains at once.

The crab only snapped its claws and scuttled down the gangplank onto the sand. Captain Ramona and Captain Basil raced after it, hopping over shells and splashing through the shallows, while their crews cheered from the rails.

At the foot of a palm tree, the crab dropped its half and vanished into a rock pool.

Ramona picked it up. Basil unfolded his own ragged half from his waistcoat. "Well, blow me down," whispered Ramona.

The two halves fitted together like puzzle pieces. A golden X shone right beneath the palm tree.

Basil's moustache drooped as he looked from the torn map to Ramona.

"Then let's share the treasure," said Ramona, and she offered him her hand.

They dug with two spades, one from each ship. Sand flew, crabs scuttled, and a few minutes later, clunk! Their spades struck a wooden chest. Inside lay sacks of gold coins, and a hundred chocolate ones wrapped in shiny foil.

"Fifty each," said Ramona, counting carefully. "And the chocolate goes to whoever can sing the loudest shanty."

Both crews sang so badly that the gulls flew away, and the parrot ended up in a sulk.

As the sun sank behind the palm trees, the two ships rocked gently side by side at anchor. Lanterns glowed like tiny moons.

Ramona yawned, and Basil yawned back, and the parrot tucked its head beneath one wing.

Hush now. The waves are soft, the confetti is sleepy, and the sea is rocking everyone to rest.

Goodnight, sailors. Goodnight, sea.

first_draft.title: Ada and Barnaby's Gate
first_draft.text:
On a warm evening that smelled of cut grass and rain, Ada sat on the back step with her wellies on the wrong feet. Something squeaked in the hedge. Then something squeaked again, a little higher and a little sadder.

Out tumbled a baby dinosaur no bigger than a laundry basket. He had a flat, rubbery beak like a duck's, a tail that swished like a paintbrush, and speckled green skin that shimmered in the lamplight. He blinked two amber eyes at Ada and said, "Hrrp?"

"Hello," whispered Ada. "I'm Ada. Who are you?"

"Hrrp," said the dinosaur. He hopped in a small circle, then stopped and stared hard at the garden gate.

"Barnaby," Ada decided. "That's your name now, if you like it." He wagged his tail so hard that a pebble flew off the path.

"Are you lost, Barnaby?" Ada asked, standing up so her wellies flapped. "Is your family on the other side of the gate?"

Barnaby hung his head and gave a long, wobbly honk. From beyond the garden wall came an answer, a deep and rumbling HOOOONK, like a foghorn that had swallowed a trumpet.

"That's your mum!" said Ada. "She's calling you home."

Barnaby squeaked with joy and charged for the gate. He bumped into the flowerpots, knocked over the watering can, and came out with a daisy stuck to his nose. Ada giggled so hard she had to hold her tummy.

"Ooh, a fancy hat," she said, when she could speak again. Barnaby shook his head, and the daisy fell off with a plop.

First, Ada tried to lift him over the wall. He was as heavy as a sack of potatoes, and she only managed a wobble and a grunt. Then she tried to push the gate, but it would not budge.

The wind picked up. The hedge rustled, and the honks grew faint and far away. Barnaby's tail drooped low, and he sat down with a sad little hrrp.

Ada looked at the gate. Its latch was a small iron loop, sitting just above her hand. "Wait," she said slowly. "Maybe it isn't locked. Maybe it's only stuck."

She wiggled the loop up, then down, then up again. Click! The gate creaked open, slow and squeaky, like a door in a storybook.

Barnaby zoomed through and out onto the lane. A tall shape moved behind the hedge, and then a gentle head with a bumpy green crest peeked over. Mum bent down with a soft hum and nuzzled Barnaby until he squeaked and wriggled with happiness.

Then she looked at Ada and let out a warm, soft honk, as if to say thank you. Ada waved. "Goodnight, Barnaby," she whispered. "Mind the puddles."

Ada tiptoed back up the step. Her wellies came off with a thump, one and then the other, and she lined them up neatly by the door. Past the hedge, the honks came softer and softer, like a lullaby played on a very big, very gentle trumpet.

The garden grew quiet. The lamplight glowed. The grass stopped rustling, and the moon rose over the wall, round and slow. Ada yawned and pulled her blanket up to her chin. Somewhere far away, a sleepy hrrp. Somewhere closer, a sleepy honk. Goodnight, garden. Goodnight, Barnaby.

first_draft.title: June and the Blue Gate
first_draft.text:
The bike stood at the bottom of the garden, shiny and red, with a bell that went ting when you tapped it. June stood beside it in her wellies, both hands on the handlebars, and wobbled.

"Ready?" asked Grandad Ivo, holding the back of the saddle with one big hand. His gardening gloves were muddy at the fingers.

"Not yet," said June. "My tummy is doing loop-the-loops."

Grandad Ivo nodded slowly, as if tummies deserved respect. "Shall we try just pushing? No pedalling, just walking together."

So they walked. The wheels crunched over the gravel path. June's wellies squeaked. A blackbird hopped along the fence, scolding them with a sharp little chook-chook. Every time June looked down at the pedals, her bike wobbled like a jelly on a plate.

"Grandad, you're holding on," she said.

"I am," he admitted. "I'll let go when you tell me."

June took a breath, all the way down to her wellies. She thought about the sofa cushions she had built into a bridge, and the way she had balanced across it without falling off. Balance was a sort of trick, she decided. You had to look ahead, not down.

"Let go," she whispered. "Just a little."

Grandad Ivo let go. The bike rolled. June pedalled once, twice, and the wheels hummed. She wobbled left, then right, then left again, and the blackbird flew off in a fright, yelping, "Oh, oh, oh!"

June giggled so hard she nearly tipped. But she didn't put her feet down. She kept her eyes on the blue gate at the end of the garden, and she kept pedalling.

"Grandad, I'm doing it!" she shouted. "Look!"

But when she looked back, Grandad Ivo was far behind, waving his gloves in the air like a cheering crowd. June wobbled again. Her heart went thump, thump, thump. She wanted to stop, and she wanted to go, both at once.

Grandad Ivo jogged up, puffing. "Feeling wobbly?"

"Mixed up," said June. "Part of me wants to go and part of me wants a cuddle."

"That's allowed," he said, and he smiled into his scratchy beard. "You can be brave and still need a rest. Shall we have a sit on the bench?"

They sat. June swung her wellies. The sun slid behind the apple tree, and the garden turned gold, then soft grey. She picked a dandelion clock and blew, and the seeds drifted away over the fence like tiny parachutes.

"Okay," she said. "Once more. Ready, Grandad."

This time June pedalled before he even reached her. She went past the rosebush, past the watering can, past the wobbly stone that always tried to trip her. She didn't look down. She looked at the blue gate, and she sailed right through it, with her hair flying and her bell going ting, ting, ting.

Grandad Ivo clapped and clapped. "June, you rode all the way to the gate!"

June rolled to a stop, her cheeks warm and pink. "I didn't fall," she said. "Not even once."

They wheeled the bike back up the path together. The lights came on in the kitchen window. The blackbird was back on the fence, very quietly now.

That night, June lay in bed with her blanket up to her chin. Her legs still felt like they were pedalling, round and round, slow and soft.

From the hallway came Grandad Ivo's whisper. "Goodnight, rider."

June smiled into her pillow. The bike was asleep in the shed, and so was the garden, and so, very gently, was she.

final.title: June and the Blue Gate
final.text:
The bike stood at the bottom of the garden, shiny and red, with a bell that went ting when you tapped it. June stood beside it in her wellies, both hands on the handlebars, and wobbled.

"Ready?" asked Grandad Ivo, holding the back of the saddle with one big hand. His gardening gloves were muddy at the fingers.

"Not yet," said June. "My tummy is doing loop-the-loops."

Grandad Ivo nodded slowly, as if tummies deserved respect. "Shall we try just pushing? No pedalling, just walking together."

So they walked. The wheels crunched over the gravel path. June's wellies squeaked. A blackbird hopped along the fence, scolding them with a sharp little chook-chook. Every time June looked down at the pedals, her bike wobbled like a jelly on a plate.

"Grandad, you're holding on," she said.

"I am," he admitted. "I'll let go when you tell me."

June took a breath, all the way down to her wellies. She thought about the sofa cushions she had built into a bridge, and the way she had balanced across it without falling off. Balance was a sort of trick, she decided. You had to look ahead, not down.

"Let go," she whispered. "Just a little."

Grandad Ivo let go. The bike rolled. June pedalled once, twice, and the wheels hummed. She wobbled left, then right, then left again, and the blackbird flew off in a fright, yelping, "Oh, oh, oh!"

June giggled so hard she nearly tipped. But she didn't put her feet down. She kept her eyes on the blue gate at the end of the garden, and she kept pedalling.

"Grandad, I'm doing it!" she shouted. "Look!"

But when she looked back, Grandad Ivo was far behind, waving his gloves in the air like a cheering crowd. June wobbled again. Her heart went thump, thump, thump. She wanted to stop, and she wanted to go, both at once.

Grandad Ivo jogged up, puffing. "Feeling wobbly?"

"Mixed up," said June. "Part of me wants to go and part of me wants a cuddle."

"That's allowed," he said, and he smiled into his scratchy beard. "You can be brave and still need a rest. Shall we have a sit on the bench?"

They sat. June swung her wellies. The sun slid behind the apple tree, and the garden turned gold, then soft grey. She picked a dandelion clock and blew, and the seeds drifted away over the fence like tiny parachutes.

"Okay," she said. "Once more. Ready, Grandad."

This time June pedalled before he even reached her. She went past the rosebush, past the watering can, past the wobbly stone that always tried to trip her. She didn't look down. She looked at the blue gate, and she sailed right through it, with her hair flying and her bell going ting, ting, ting.

Grandad Ivo clapped and clapped. "June, you rode all the way to the gate!"

June rolled to a stop, her cheeks warm and pink. "I didn't fall," she said. "Not even once."

They wheeled the bike back up the path together. The lights came on in the kitchen window. The blackbird was back on the fence, very quietly now.

That night, June lay in bed with her blanket up to her chin. Her legs still felt like they were pedalling, round and round, slow and soft.

From the hallway came Grandad Ivo's whisper. "Goodnight, rider."

June smiled into her pillow. The bike was asleep in the shed, and so was the garden, and so, very gently, was she.

first_draft.title: Pemberton and the Shrinking Puddle
first_draft.text:
Pemberton was a scruffy brown dog with a curly tail, and he loved puddles more than anything in the whole wide world.

Every morning he trotted down Pebble Lane to visit them. There was a wide puddle outside the bakery, a skinny one beside the mailbox, and a round, deep one under the old oak tree. That one was his favorite. Its water was as shiny as a spoon, and it wobbled whenever a leaf landed on it.

"Splish, splash, sploosh!" Pemberton would say, though he really only said it with his tail.

One soggy Tuesday, his friend Umi came along in her yellow raincoat. She carried a bright green bucket and wore a worried face.

"Pemberton," she said, "your puddle is shrinking."

He stopped and looked. The round puddle was smaller than yesterday. Its edges had turned pale and crinkly, like the top of a cooling pie. The sun had been drinking it up, one warm sip at a time.

Pemberton sat down with a small, sad whine. His ears drooped nearly to the ground.

Umi crouched beside him and tapped her chin. "Puddles don't last forever," she said. "But maybe we can help this one last a little longer."

"How?" Pemberton asked. It came out as a grumble.

Umi looked up at the sky, then at the tall wooden fence, then at the big branches of the oak. "The sun is hitting it right in the middle," she said slowly. "If we could give it some shade..."

They searched the garden shed. Umi found a floppy square of cardboard and a long, bendy stick. Pemberton found a sock. It was a very smelly sock, and he was very proud of it, though it wasn't much use for shade.

Umi propped the cardboard on the stick and tucked the end under a low branch. It made a little roof over the puddle. When a breeze blew, the cardboard creaked, and Pemberton jumped back with a yelp. He sniffed it carefully, wagged twice, and decided it was only cardboard after all.

The next morning, the puddle was still there. It was not as big as before, but it was not as small as it could have been. Pemberton was so pleased that he did a happy spin.

Then came a loud, cheerful noise. "Quack! Quack! Quack!"

Around the corner waddled a family of ducks. There was a fat mother duck and five fluffy ducklings, all following in a wobbly line. They had been searching for water too, and they went straight to the puddle, dipping their beaks in with happy little splashes.

Pemberton's tail stopped wagging. He took a step forward, then a step back. This was his puddle. He had loved it first. A small, grumbly feeling rumbled in his tummy.

Umi didn't say anything. She just sat on the curb and watched, with her chin in her hands.

Pemberton looked at the ducklings. One of them had lost its balance and was flapping at the edge, trying to climb out of the mud. Pemberton padded over, nudged it gently with his nose, and moved his big muddy paw aside so it had room to stand. The little duckling hopped onto the grass, shook itself, and quacked a thank-you.

Pemberton watched them splash for a while. Then he trotted to the far side of the puddle and let the ducks have the middle. Splish, splash went the ducklings, and their ripples bumped into his paws.

Umi laughed and stomped her yellow boots in the shallow edge. Splish! Pemberton barked, and the ducks quacked back, and for a moment the whole lane sounded like a party.

That evening, the sun slipped down behind the oak tree. The cardboard roof was tucked away in the shed. The ducks had waddled off into the reeds. The puddle lay still and dark, and a silver moon floated in it.

Pemberton curled up on the cool grass beside it. His tail rested over his nose. Somewhere a frog began to hum, low and slow.

Umi yawned and tiptoed home, her green bucket swinging softly at her side.

Pemberton sighed a sleepy sigh. The moon rested on the water, quiet as a secret.

"Goodnight, puddle," he whispered. "Goodnight."

first_draft.title: Octavia and the Quiet Latch
first_draft.text:
The night train left the station with a long, sleepy sigh, as if it, too, was ready for bed. Golden lamps slid past the window, then the town folded itself up into darkness, and the stars came out one by one like tiny lanterns being lit. Octavia pressed her nose to the cool glass and watched them.

She was seven years old, and this was the longest journey she had ever taken. Her grandmother had dozed off almost at once, her knitting resting in her lap like a sleeping grey cat. Octavia wiggled her toes inside her woolly socks. The velvet seat was soft, the wheels hummed beneath her, and the carriage rocked gently from side to side. Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Hush, hush, the train seemed to say.

Octavia yawned, and a yawn is catching, so she yawned again. Across the narrow aisle sat an old man named Mr. Rafferty, with a tartan blanket over his knees and a small brown dog snoring at his feet. Every so often, a brass latch above his seat gave a tiny rattle. Tick. Tap. Tick. Each time, Mr. Rafferty sighed and shifted, and each time his eyes opened a little wider.

"I can't seem to settle," he whispered, rubbing his eyes. "That latch has been knocking since the last station. It's like a clock that forgot how to stop."

Octavia looked up. The latch was loose, and whenever the train swayed, it tapped against the window frame. It was not a loud sound. But in the middle of the night, it was just loud enough to keep a tired man awake.

Octavia thought about it the way her grandmother thought about a tangled ball of wool, slowly, turning it over and over. She could not fix the train, and she could not make it stop swaying. But in her bag she had a soft blue scarf, long and woolly and smelling faintly of lavender. Perhaps a scarf could be a pillow for a rattling latch.

She tiptoed across the aisle, careful not to wake her grandmother. "May I try something?" she asked. Mr. Rafferty smiled and held her elbow while she stood on tiptoe. Octavia wound the scarf twice around the loose latch and tucked the ends into the gap by the frame, pressing gently, the way you tuck in a sleepy kitten. Then she let go.

They waited. The train swayed left. The train swayed right. Tick... and nothing. No tap came. The scarf had hushed the latch as softly as a hand over a mouth. Mr. Rafferty let out a long breath, and his shoulders dropped. "Well, now," he murmured. "That is the nicest quiet I have heard all week." The little brown dog lifted one ear, gave a contented grunt, and went back to snoring.

Just then, a conductor came along the corridor, swinging a silver lantern. Her name was Sybil. Her hair was pinned up with a silver comb, and her navy coat had shiny buttons that caught the light. She peered at the scarf and laughed softly. "Well done, young lady. This train has been rattling for three stations, and nobody has solved it until now." Then she handed Octavia a small paper cup of warm milk with a pinch of nutmeg on top. Octavia sipped it slowly, feeling warm all the way down.

Outside, the night was changing. The stars were thinning above the hills, and the hills rolled by like great sleeping animals with soft, dark backs. A farmhouse window glowed once, then went dark. An owl called from a faraway wood, hoo, hoo, and the train answered with a long, low whistle that rolled across the fields and faded away. Octavia rested her cheek against the window and felt her eyelids grow heavy.

She tiptoed back to her seat and climbed beneath the blanket beside her grandmother. Without waking, her grandmother murmured, "Good girl," and patted her hand. The carriage was dimmer now, the lamps turned low to a honey glow. Across the aisle, Mr. Rafferty's breathing slowed, and the little dog sighed in his sleep.

The wheels turned slowly, carrying everyone through the dark. Clickety... clack... Hush now... The latch was quiet. The lamps were soft. The moon slipped behind a cloud, and the hills kept their secrets. Octavia's eyes drifted closed, and the last thing she heard was the gentle rocking of the night train.

Goodnight, little train. Goodnight, sleepy hills. Goodnight, Octavia.

She was seven years old, and this was the longest journey she had ever taken. Her grandmother had dozed off almost at once, her knitting resting in her lap like a sleeping grey cat. Octavia wiggled her toes inside her woolly socks. The velvet seat was soft, the wheels hummed beneath her, and the carriage rocked gently from side to side. Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Hush, hush, the train seemed to say.

Octavia yawned, and a yawn is catching, so she yawned again. Across the narrow aisle sat an old man named Mr. Rafferty, with a tartan blanket over his knees and a small brown dog snoring at his feet. Every so often, a brass latch above his seat gave a tiny rattle. Tick. Tap. Tick. Each time, Mr. Rafferty sighed and shifted, and each time his eyes opened a little wider.

"I can't seem to settle," he whispered, rubbing his eyes. "That latch has been knocking since the last station. It's like a clock that forgot how to stop."

Octavia looked up. The latch was loose, and whenever the train swayed, it tapped against the window frame. It was not a loud sound. But in the middle of the night, it was just loud enough to keep a tired man awake.

Octavia thought about it the way her grandmother thought about a tangled ball of wool, slowly, turning it over and over. She could not fix the train, and she could not make it stop swaying. But in her bag she had a soft blue scarf, long and woolly and smelling faintly of lavender. Perhaps a scarf could be a pillow for a rattling latch.

She tiptoed across the aisle, careful not to wake her grandmother. "May I try something?" she asked. Mr. Rafferty smiled and held her elbow while she stood on tiptoe. Octavia wound the scarf twice around the loose latch and tucked the ends into the gap by the frame, pressing gently, the way you tuck in a sleepy kitten. Then she let go.

They waited. The train swayed left. The train swayed right. Tick... and nothing. No tap came. The scarf had hushed the latch as softly as a hand over a mouth. Mr. Rafferty let out a long breath, and his shoulders dropped. "Well, now," he murmured. "That is the nicest quiet I have heard all week." The little brown dog lifted one ear, gave a contented grunt, and went back to snoring.

Just then, a conductor came along the corridor, swinging a silver lantern. Her name was Sybil. Her hair was pinned up with a silver comb, and her navy coat had shiny buttons that caught the light. She peered at the scarf and laughed softly. "Well done, young lady. This train has been rattling for three stations, and nobody has solved it until now." Then she handed Octavia a small paper cup of warm milk with a pinch of nutmeg on top. Octavia sipped it slowly, feeling warm all the way down.

Outside, the night was changing. The stars were thinning above the hills, and the hills rolled by like great sleeping animals with soft, dark backs. A farmhouse window glowed once, then went dark. An owl called from a faraway wood, hoo, hoo, and the train answered with a long, low whistle that rolled across the fields and faded away. Octavia rested her cheek against the window and felt her eyelids grow heavy.

She tiptoed back to her seat and climbed beneath the blanket beside her grandmother. Without waking, her grandmother murmured, "Good girl," and patted her hand. The carriage was dimmer now, the lamps turned low to a honey glow. Across the aisle, Mr. Rafferty's breathing slowed, and the little dog sighed in his sleep.

The wheels turned slowly, carrying everyone through the dark. Clickety... clack... Hush now... The latch was quiet. The lamps were soft. The moon slipped behind a cloud, and the hills kept their secrets. Octavia's eyes drifted closed, and the last thing she heard was the gentle rocking of the night train.

Goodnight, little train. Goodnight, sleepy hills. Goodnight, Octavia.
